title: Phone Stands for Stiff Hands: A Plush Pillow or a Magnetic Stand?
subtitle: Two very different kinds of phone stand, what each one offers, and where each falls short.
excerpt: If holding a phone makes your hands ache, a stand may let you set it down instead. Here is how a soft pillow stand compares with a magnetic charging stand, and what neither can promise.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Holding a phone seems simple until your hands start to object. Squeezing a slim slab of glass for a long video call or a chapter of an e-book can leave fingers and wrists sore, especially for people with arthritis. UCLA Health notes that nearly 60 million American adults have some form of arthritis, and about two million Americans with arthritis say it limits their ability to grasp small objects.
The good news is that you do not always have to hold the phone at all. A stand can hold it for you while you watch or read, so your hands only need to tap, swipe or rest.
"The problem is that our thumbs play a role in about 50% of all hand functions." (UCLA Health, "Can texting give you arthritis?", April 2022)
How a stand helps, and the two main kinds

UCLA Health suggests putting the phone down while texting, resting your thumbs, using a stylus or voice-to-text (which lets you speak a message instead of typing it), and using a removable grip that lets your fingers hold the phone. UCLA also says to see a doctor for ongoing hand pain or stiffness. A Gulf News article, which is undated and which we have only seen in part, quotes a rheumatology specialist saying a phone stand can help when watching videos or reading because it reduces continuous gripping.
The two products below take quite different routes.

The PhoneSpud is a soft, plush stand with a phone pocket, meant for resting the phone on a lap or table. The maker says it works with any phone, and it can stand horizontally or vertically. The trade-off is bulk: its weight and zipper pocket add size, and it does not help when you are walking around or holding the phone out at arm's length.

The Belkin is a magnetic stand that converts to a charging pad, with adjustable tilt in either mode. It charges wirelessly, meaning without plugging a cord into the phone. The phone needs a magnetic Qi2 or MagSafe-compatible case to stick, and a bare phone will not stay on. Belkin's page describes a charger and stand first. It says nothing about hand comfort.

items: Where you use the phone most. A pillow suits a lap, a bed or a recliner; a stand like the Belkin suits a table or nightstand.
Case compatibility. The Belkin needs a magnetic case. The PhoneSpud is listed as working with any phone.
Charging. The PhoneSpud comes with a 10,000 mAh power bank (a portable battery), and the Belkin charges an iPhone or a compatible Samsung while it holds it.
Bulk. The PhoneSpud's weight and zipper pocket add size, so think about whether you can move it easily.

Price, sales and stock. The PhoneSpud sale prices were labeled Back to School on a saved copy of the page and may have ended, and its colors showed as sold out or unavailable. Check the current price, stock and return policy before ordering.
No monthly fees. Neither product lists any ongoing fee.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well

For a pillow stand, pick the one spot where you most often read or watch, such as a favorite chair or bed, and keep it there. Slide the phone into the pocket and use the charging port if you want to keep the phone powered.
For a magnetic stand, put the magnetic case on the phone first and confirm it snaps on firmly. Place the stand near an outlet on a stable surface. Then set the phone against it whenever you sit down.
Whichever you choose, voice-to-text is one of the fixes UCLA Health suggests, and it pairs naturally with a stand.

A stand or pillow does not treat arthritis. PhoneSpuds markets its pillow for arthritis and hand pain, but those are the maker's own claims, and neither product has independent testing on hand comfort. A stand will not help while you are walking around or holding the phone out. If hand pain or stiffness keeps coming back, talk with your doctor.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: If you are shopping for a parent who texts a lot or watches videos in bed, a stand may be worth considering, though neither of these has been shown to ease sore hands. Think about where they sit, what case they use, and whether they can still get the phone onto it. The right choice is usually the one they will actually reach for.
